title: Welcome To A New Branch Of Quantum Computing!
text:
“Out of the void arises matter, just as out of silence emerges an idea.”
— Professor Alvin




Welcome, Fellow Explorers!
Whether you are a seasoned quantum physicist, a curious software engineer, a student wandering through the fringes of the web, or simply someone fascinated by the architecture of reality: welcome aboard.
You have just stepped into an open laboratory dedicated to an unconventional scientific journey. Here, we step away from traditional silicon chips and ultra-cold cryostats to explore how the elegant, subtle geometry of conjugated carbon systems could form the backbone of a radically different kind of quantum processor. Make yourself comfortable, bring your curiosity, and let’s explore what happens when we look at matter through the lens of computation.



How I Work
The bulk of this research has been conducted over the years using nothing more than a simple graphite pencil and stacks of paper. I find it deeply amusing that the very same carbon atoms I smear across a sheet of paper might one day, if arranged with enough precision, form a quantum supercomputer.
This website is the digital transcription of my physical laboratory notebook, and I will continue adding new findings as time permits. It is an evolving work in progress.
Scientific inquiry consists of sudden bursts of euphoria followed by long, quiet stretches of rumination. Do not be discouraged if updates pause for long intervals; that downtime is simply the recharge cycle my neurons require before taking the next quantum leap.



A Disclaimer on the Speculation / Wild Thoughts Section
The creative phase of scientific discovery is often anything but strictly scientific. True inspiration can strike from the most unexpected corners of reality.
The Speculations section at the bottom of each article exists so I can think out loud without self-censorship. Any idea is welcome there, provided it has a conceptual thread connecting it to the topic at hand — and above all, the spark needed to ignite novel ways of thinking.
A fair warning: If your sensibilities are offended by free-form intuition that casually weaves rigorous science, spaghetti sauce, space aliens, and unicorns into the same conceptual thought experiment—skip that section entirely!



House Rules for Discussions & Feedback
You are warmly invited to comment, debate, and constructively critique any post. To keep this space constructive and enjoyable to read, please adhere to a single cardinal rule:

Ad hominem attacks are strictly forbidden. Ideas, however, can be attacked as fiercely and relentlessly as you wish.

Bring your sharpest arguments, not your personal grievances.



The Road Ahead
It is important to emphasize that the work presented across these notes remains firmly in the theoretical realm. While these concepts are explored with analytical depth, their real-world physical implementation will demand significant experimental and technological breakthroughs. Scaling and testing them will inevitably reveal growing layers of complexity, demanding both deep interdisciplinary synergy and sustained reflection.
And yet, despite all the underlying complexity… the fundamental rules are so strikingly intuitive that a five-year-old could grasp them without breaking a sweat.

Logical States
Before diving into the fascinating realm of quantum logic, mastering the fundamentals of classical logic and traditional logic gates is essential.
Logic gates are the foundational building blocks of digital electronics and modern computing. They manipulate binary signals—units of information represented by bits that take one of two distinct values: “0” (false, low, off) or “1” (true, high, on).
Throughout this blog, we will express all circuits in matrix form. So, we might as well get comfortable with this concept right from the start.
We define the logical states as:
\[
\text{ZERO} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
\]
and
\[
\text{ONE} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\]



Logical Gates
Basic logic gates are the elementary building blocks of any digital system. These gates are: NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR, XOR, and XNOR. Each gate exhibits a specific behavior, formally defined by a truth table that maps its inputs to its output.

Matrix representation
You might be wondering what all these matrices actually contain. You can think of a matrix as a “box” that embodies a function.
They all share the exact same format:
- The rows correspond to an enumeration of all possible input combinations.
- The columns correspond to an enumeration of all possible output combinations.
If a function has \(M\) binary inputs and \(N\) binary outputs, the resulting matrix will have \(2^M\) rows and \(2^N\) columns.
The column containing the value 1 marks the precise spot where a given input maps to its corresponding output.
For example, here is the matrix representation of the AND gate with the rows and column labels added:


\[ \begin{array}{r|cc|} \text{} & \text{``0''} & \text{``1''} \\  \hline \text{``00''} & 1 & 0 \\ \text{``01''} & 1 & 0 \\ \text{``10''} & 1 & 0 \\ \text{``11''} & 0 & 1 \\  \hline \end{array} \]


As expected, the output is 1, only if both inputs are 1.
Even the logical states follow the same format. You can think of a logical state as a function with zero input and one output (the logical state).
Logical 0:


\[ \begin{array}{|cc|} \text{``0''} & \text{``1''} \\  \hline 1 & 0 \\  \hline \end{array} \]


Logical 1:


\[ \begin{array}{|cc|} \text{``0''} & \text{``1''} \\  \hline 0 & 1 \\  \hline \end{array} \]





Matrix arithmetic
The beauty of this representation is that functions can be chained together end-to-end using standard matrix multiplication.
For example, if we have a state corresponding to the bit “1” and pass it through a NOT gate, we can simply compute: \(\text{One} \cdot \text{NOT}\).


\[  \begin{array}{|cc|}  \hline 0 & 1 \\  \hline \end{array}  \cdot  \begin{array}{|cc|}  \hline 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\  \hline \end{array}  =  \begin{array}{|cc|}  \hline 1 & 0 \\  \hline \end{array}  \]


And this yields the expected result: Zero.
For logic gates with two inputs, \(A\) and \(B\), one might naively expect something like \(A \cdot B \cdot \text{AND}\). However, that will not work dimensionally. \(A\) and \(B\) are \(1 \times 2\) matrices, whereas the \(\text{AND}\) gate is a \(4 \times 2\) matrix.
To give the inputs \((A, B)\) the proper dimension to interface with the AND gate, they must first be combined using the Kronecker tensor product (\(A \otimes B\)).


\[  \begin{array}{|cc|} \text{``0''} & \text{``1''} \\  \hline 1 & 0 \\  \hline \end{array}  \otimes  \begin{array}{|cc|} \text{``0''} & \text{``1''} \\  \hline 0 & 1 \\  \hline \end{array}  =  \begin{array}{|cccc|} \text{``00''} & \text{``01''} & \text{``10''} & \text{``11''} \\  \hline 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\  \hline \end{array}  \]


Once the inputs are combined into a single matrix, we can multiply them directly by the logic gate:


\[  \begin{array}{|cccc|} \text{``00''} & \text{``01''} & \text{``10''} & \text{``11''} \\  \hline 0 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\  \hline \end{array}  \cdot  \begin{array}{r|cc|} \text{} & \text{``0''} & \text{``1''} \\  \hline \text{``00''} & 1 & 0 \\ \text{``01''} & 1 & 0 \\ \text{``10''} & 1 & 0 \\ \text{``11''} & 0 & 1 \\  \hline \end{array}  =  \begin{array}{|cc|} \text{``0''} & \text{``1''} \\  \hline 0 & 1 \\  \hline \end{array}  \]

title: About The Author
text:
I am an independent researcher pursuing a new paradigm in quantum information: computing built directly upon the physics of conjugated carbon bonds.
I graduated with a B.Sc. in Computer Science from the Université de Montréal in 1997. Over the decades, my path has taken me through the complete stack of computation—from discrete transistor electronics and microprocessor design up to low-level assembly and modern high-level languages.
Investigating carbon-based quantum logic naturally forced me outside traditional silos, driving me to dive into chemistry, biology, mathematics, and physics. While I feel I have only scratched the surface of these vast disciplines, this journey has shaped my approach into one driven entirely by systems thinking.
Beyond the terminal and the lab bench, my thinking is anchored in the philosophical foundations of deep ecology. I actively explore radical alternatives for future societies — questioning our relationship with the living world, re-evaluating technological necessity, and seeking systemic pathways to genuinely improve how we inhabit this Earth.
